blocks.text: Alkenes · Alkynes · Benzene · Methylbenzene. Built around the questions that come up in tests: what is asked, what to write, and the traps.

items: Name / draw alkenes, alkynes, dienes, benzene derivatives (lowest number to the multiple bond).
Prepare an alkene: alcoholic KOH from halogenoalkane; conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 170 °C from ethanol (140 °C = ether).
Predict the major product: Markovnikov, Zaitsev, and the peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) exception.
Test for unsaturation (bromine water) and for a terminal alkyne (ammoniacal Cu(I): red; Ag(I): white).
Ozonolysis: what carbonyl compounds come out.
Why benzene substitutes instead of adding; resonance energy −360 − (−208) = −152 kJ/mol.
Mechanism of electrophilic substitution: generate E<sup>+</sup>, attack, lose H<sup>+</sup> (nitration, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts).
Reagents and conditions for nitration, sulphonation, alkylation, acylation.
Methylbenzene: ring (AlCl<sub>3</sub>/HNO<sub>3</sub>) vs side chain (Cl<sub>2</sub>/UV); TNT; oxidation to benzoic acid.

blocks.text: A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C). General formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>. Carbons of the C=C are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. Unsaturated.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C). General formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n-2</sub>. Also called acetylenes. Carbons are sp hybridised (linear). Highly unsaturated.
An alkene containing two C=C. Conjugated diene: C=C–C=C (double bonds separated by one single bond), e.g. buta-1,3-diene. Allene: C=C=C.
A compound containing C=C or C≡C that can undergo addition; decolourises bromine water.
A hydrocarbon with a highly stable unsaturated ring structure, benzene and its derivatives. Benzene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: a planar ring with delocalised electrons.
Formed by replacing one or more hydrogens of benzene by other atoms or groups (e.g. –CH<sub>3</sub>, –Cl, –COOH, –NO<sub>2</sub>).
Two reactants combine to give one product, the C=C or C≡C is used up (typical of alkenes and alkynes).
Addition started by an electron-poor species (electrophile) attacking the electron-rich C=C or C≡C.
An electrophile replaces a hydrogen on the benzene ring while the ring stays intact (typical of benzene).
A species that is attracted to electron-rich areas and accepts an electron pair (e.g. NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, Cl<sup>+</sup>, R<sup>+</sup>, H<sup>+</sup>).
An electron-pair acceptor (AlCl<sub>3</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>, AlBr<sub>3</sub>) that polarises a halogen molecule or alkyl/acyl halide to generate the electrophile.
When an unsymmetrical reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the positive part of the reagent adds to the carbon of the double bond that already has more hydrogen atoms.
Opposite orientation, occurs for HBr in the presence of an organic peroxide (ROOR).
In elimination, the more substituted alkene is the major product.
Addition of H<sub>2</sub> / of X<sub>2</sub> / of water (steam, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> catalyst) across the multiple bond.
Addition of two OH groups across C=C using an oxidising agent (alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) to give a diol.
Reaction of an alkene with ozone (O<sub>3</sub>) giving an ozonide (explosive, not isolated), hydrolysed to aldehydes / ketones.
A cyclic ether, e.g. epoxyethane from ethene + O<sub>2</sub> over silver at 250 °C.
Many alkene monomers join to form a polymer of very high relative molecular mass (n CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> → –(CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>n</sub>–).
An alkyne with the triple bond at the end of the chain (≡C–H); its hydrogen is weakly acidic and forms dicarbides with Cu(I) (red) and Ag(I) (white).
True structure is a blend of canonical (Kekulé) forms of equal energy with no charge separation; all six C–C bonds in benzene are identical in length.
The extra stability gained by delocalisation of electrons in benzene: −360 − (−208) = −152 kJ/mol (176 kJ/mol using bond-enthalpy data).
Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> + concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; generates NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>.
Positions 1,2 / 1,3 / 1,4 on a disubstituted benzene ring.
Reaction of an arene with a halogenoalkane (alkylation) or acyl halide (acylation) using AlCl<sub>3</sub> to give an alkylbenzene or aromatic ketone.

rows: alkane stem, -ane → -ene; number so the C=C gets the LOWEST number; then substituents alphabetically
-ane → -yne, same numbering rule. HC≡CH ethyne; but-1-yne and but-2-yne are isomers (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)

lines: Trap: numbering from the wrong end. Multiple bond gets the lowest number FIRST.

blocks.title: Name a substituted diene
blocks.task: Give the IUPAC name of CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>.
steps: Choose the longest chain containing both double bonds: four carbons, so the parent is buta-diene.
Number from the end that gives the multiple bonds the lowest numbers: the double bonds are at 1 and 3.
The methyl substituent is attached to carbon 2.
blocks.answer: 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene.

blocks.text: Alkenes react by addition: the C=C breaks open and two new atoms join on. Preparations are listed first, then the reactions.

rows: Zaitsev: more substituted alkene is major
Br<sub>2</sub> (in CCl<sub>4</sub> or bromine water), room temp
conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, warm; then heat with water
splits the C=C into two C=O

blocks.title: Markovnikov: propene + HBr
blocks.task: Give the major product when propene reacts with HBr (no peroxide).
steps: Draw it: CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>. Look at the two carbons of the double bond.
Count the hydrogens on each: CH has 1 H; CH<sub>2</sub> has 2 H.
Rule: the positive part (H) goes to the carbon that already has MORE hydrogens, so H goes to CH<sub>2</sub>.
The negative part (Br) goes to the other carbon, the CH.
blocks.answer: CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> (2-bromopropane). With a peroxide present the product flips to CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (1-bromopropane).

blocks.title: Zaitsev: elimination from 2-chlorobutane
blocks.task: Name the major and minor alkenes from 2-chlorobutane with alcoholic KOH.
steps: Draw CH<sub>3</sub>–CHCl–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>. The carbon with Cl is C2; its neighbours are C1 (CH<sub>3</sub>) and C3 (CH<sub>2</sub>).
Remove HCl: take H from C3 → C=C between C2 and C3 → but-2-ene. Take H from C1 → but-1-ene.
Zaitsev: the more substituted C=C (more alkyl groups on it) is the major product. But-2-ene has two alkyl groups; but-1-ene has one.
blocks.answer: but-2-ene (major), but-1-ene (minor).

try_it.question: 1-chlorobutane + alcoholic KOH
try_it.answer: only but-1-ene (only one neighbouring carbon, C2, has H).

blocks.title: Ozonolysis: where does the C=C split?
blocks.task: Give the products of CH<sub>3</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + O<sub>3</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O.
steps: Mark the C=C: it is between C2 (carrying two CH<sub>3</sub>-type groups) and C3 (carrying H and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>).
Break the double bond and put =O on each carbon that was in it.
Left piece: CH<sub>3</sub>–C(=O)–CH<sub>3</sub> (no H on that carbon, so a KETONE: propanone).
Right piece: O=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (has an H, so an ALDEHYDE: propanal).
blocks.answer: propanone + propanal.

blocks.title: Choose the conditions: ethanol → ethene or ether?
blocks.task: A student heats ethanol with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 140 °C hoping to make ethene. What forms?
steps: Temperature decides: 170 °C removes water from ONE ethanol molecule (alkene).
At 140 °C two ethanol molecules lose one water between them (ether).
blocks.answer: ethoxyethane CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, not ethene. Use 170 °C for ethene.

blocks.title: Ethene → ethanol in two ways
blocks.task: Show two routes from ethene to ethanol.
steps: Route 1 (direct hydration): CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH using steam, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>/SiO<sub>2</sub> catalyst, 300 °C.

Route 2 (via sulphate): CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (warm) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OSO<sub>3</sub>H, then heat with water: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OSO<sub>3</sub>H + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
blocks.answer: both give ethanol; Route 2 regenerates the acid.

blocks.title: Test: how to tell hexane from hex-1-ene
blocks.task: Describe a chemical test.
steps: Add bromine water (orange-brown) to each, shake.
Hex-1-ene has C=C, so Br<sub>2</sub> adds across it and the colour disappears.
Hexane has no C=C, so the colour stays.
blocks.answer: decolourises = hex-1-ene; no change = hexane.

sections.title: Reactions of alkynes (C≡C: addition, plus acidic ≡C–H)

rows: HBr (100 °C); HI at room temp; HCl needs HgCl<sub>2</sub>
Markovnikov; order HF < HCl < HBr < HI
RED copper dicarbide: test for terminal ≡C–H

blocks.title: Ethyne with excess HBr
blocks.task: Give the final product of ethyne + excess HBr.
steps: First addition: HC≡CH + HBr → CH<sub>2</sub>=CHBr (bromoethene).
Second addition uses Markovnikov: in CH<sub>2</sub>=CHBr the CH<sub>2</sub> has more H, so H adds to CH<sub>2</sub>.
Br adds to the carbon that already has a Br.
blocks.answer: CH<sub>3</sub>CHBr<sub>2</sub> (1,1-dibromoethane): both bromines on the same carbon.

blocks.title: Distinguish ethane, ethene and ethyne
blocks.task: Describe tests to tell the three gases apart.
steps: Test 1: bubble each through bromine water. Ethane: stays orange. Ethene and ethyne: decolourise.
Test 2: bubble the two that decolourised through ammoniacal copper(I) chloride.
Ethyne has a terminal ≡C–H: red precipitate. Ethene: no precipitate.
blocks.answer: ethane = no change in Br<sub>2</sub> water; ethene = Br<sub>2</sub> decolourised, no red ppt; ethyne = Br<sub>2</sub> decolourised and red ppt.

try_it.question: but-1-yne vs but-2-yne
try_it.answer: ammoniacal Cu(I)/Ag(I): but-1-yne gives a precipitate (terminal ≡C–H); but-2-yne gives none.

blocks.title: Make ethyne and prove it is ethyne
blocks.task: Describe preparation and one test.
steps: Add water drop by drop to a small lump of calcium dicarbide: CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>.
Collect the colourless gas. It burns with a smoky, sooty flame (high carbon content).
Bubble it through ammoniacal copper(I) chloride: a red precipitate of copper(I) dicarbide forms.
blocks.answer: ethyne confirmed by smoky flame + red precipitate.

blocks.title: Ethyne → ethanal, and ethyne → nitrobenzene (multi-step)
blocks.task: Show the reagents for each.
steps: Ethanal: HC≡CH + H<sub>2</sub>O with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and HgSO<sub>4</sub> at 60 °C → CH<sub>3</sub>CHO.
Benzene: heat ethyne at 400 °C: 3C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.
Nitrobenzene: benzene + conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> / conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 55–60 °C → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O.
blocks.answer: three steps, three sets of conditions.

blocks.title: Big idea
lines: Benzene has a stable, delocalised ring. It prefers SUBSTITUTION (ring survives) to ADDITION (ring destroyed). Addition only happens under harsh conditions.

blocks.text: 4A. Substitution (the common ones)
4B. Addition (only with harsh conditions)
4C. Methylbenzene (toluene) reactions

rows: CH<sub>2</sub>Cl → CH<sub>2</sub>OH; CHCl<sub>2</sub> → CHO; CCl<sub>3</sub> → COOH
(arrows only in notes; usual: aqueous NaOH, heat)

blocks.title: Nitration of benzene, with mechanism
blocks.task: Write reagents, conditions and mechanism for benzene → nitrobenzene.
steps: Reagents: concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> + concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (the nitrating mixture), 55–60 °C.
Make the electrophile: HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.
The benzene ring uses a pair of its π electrons to attack NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>; an intermediate forms with H and NO<sub>2</sub> on the same carbon (positive charge over the ring).
HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> takes H<sup>+</sup> away; the ring becomes aromatic again.
blocks.answer: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> (nitrobenzene) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> regenerated. A second nitration gives 1,3-dinitrobenzene.

blocks.title: Chlorination: pick the right conditions
blocks.task: What happens when Cl<sub>2</sub> reacts with (a) benzene + AlCl<sub>3</sub>, (b) benzene + UV, (c) methylbenzene + UV, (d) methylbenzene + AlCl<sub>3</sub>?
steps: Catalyst (AlCl<sub>3</sub> or Fe) means a ring SUBSTITUTION using Cl<sup>+</sup>.
UV light on benzene means ADDITION by free radicals.
UV light on methylbenzene attacks the CH<sub>3</sub> side chain (free radical substitution).
blocks.answer: (a) chlorobenzene + HCl. (b) C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>. (c) C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl, then CHCl<sub>2</sub>, CCl<sub>3</sub>. (d) chloromethylbenzenes on the ring (2- and 4-).

blocks.title: Friedel-Crafts acylation: benzene → phenylethanone
blocks.task: Give reagents and mechanism.
steps: Reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>COCl (ethanoyl chloride) and AlCl<sub>3</sub>, 50 °C.
AlCl<sub>3</sub> pulls off Cl: CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> (the electrophile).
Ring attacks CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>, giving the intermediate.
AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> takes H<sup>+</sup>: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> + HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> (catalyst back).
blocks.answer: phenylethanone, an aromatic ketone. For alkylation use CH<sub>3</sub>Cl / AlCl<sub>3</sub> under reflux instead, giving methylbenzene.

blocks.title: Methylbenzene → TNT
blocks.task: Show the route and explain why the ring reacts easily.
steps: Conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> / conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, 55–60 °C gives 2-nitromethylbenzene and 4-nitromethylbenzene.
Further nitration places a third NO<sub>2</sub>: 2,4,6-trinitromethylbenzene.
The CH<sub>3</sub> group activates the ring, so substitution is easier than for benzene.
blocks.answer: TNT (2,4,6-trinitromethylbenzene), an explosive.

blocks.title: Methylbenzene → benzoic acid
blocks.task: Give the sequence from methylbenzene.
steps: Cl<sub>2</sub> / UV light replaces side-chain H atoms: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (then CHCl<sub>2</sub>, CCl<sub>3</sub>).
Hydrolysis converts CH<sub>2</sub>Cl to CH<sub>2</sub>OH (benzyl alcohol).
Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, reflux oxidises the alcohol to benzaldehyde, then to benzoic acid.
blocks.answer: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH. (CCl<sub>3</sub> hydrolysed directly also gives COOH.)

blocks.title: Prove benzene is not three ordinary C=C bonds
blocks.task: Use the hydrogenation data.
steps: Cyclohexene + H<sub>2</sub> gives ΔH = −120 kJ/mol (one C=C).
Three separate C=C would give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ/mol.
Measured ΔH for benzene + 3H<sub>2</sub> is only −208 kJ/mol.
Difference: −360 − (−208) = −152 kJ/mol: benzene is more stable because its electrons are delocalised (resonance energy).
blocks.answer: 152 kJ/mol more stable than a three-double-bond structure.

blocks.title: Markovnikov
lines: When an unsymmetrical reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the positive part of the reagent adds to the carbon of the double bond that already has more hydrogen atoms.

blocks.title: Zaitsev
lines: In elimination the more substituted alkene is the major product: 2-chlorobutane + alcoholic KOH → but-2-ene (major), but-1-ene (minor).

blocks.title: Unsaturation test
lines: Bromine water (or Br<sub>2</sub> in CCl<sub>4</sub>) is decolourised by C=C or C≡C. Benzene does NOT decolourise it.

blocks.text: Ozonolysis products (they love this)

blocks.title: Predict an ozonolysis product
blocks.task: Predict the products when but-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with O<sub>3</sub> and is then hydrolysed with water.
steps: Locate the C=C bond and split the molecule at that bond.
Put a C=O group on each of the two carbons that were in the double bond.
Each side has one H and one CH<sub>3</sub> group, so each carbonyl product is an aldehyde.
blocks.answer: Two molecules of ethanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO.

rows: ethyne: RED ppt (copper dicarbide); ethene: none
benzene: no reaction; cyclohexene: both decolourised

blocks.text: Order for ethene / ethyne / benzene: bromine water (ethene, ethyne decolourise; benzene no) → ammoniacal Cu(I) (ethyne red ppt).

blocks.title: Distinguish ethene, ethyne and benzene
blocks.task: Give a sequence of tests that identifies each of the three compounds.
steps: Add bromine water to separate samples. The sample that does not decolourise it is benzene; ethene and ethyne decolourise it.
Test the two samples that decolourised bromine water with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride.
A red precipitate identifies ethyne; the sample with no precipitate is ethene.
blocks.answer: Benzene: bromine water shows no change. Ethene: decolourises bromine water, then no red precipitate. Ethyne: decolourises bromine water and gives a red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu(I) chloride.

blocks.title: Why substitution, not addition?
lines: Addition would destroy the delocalised π system and lose about 152 kJ/mol of stabilisation, so benzene keeps its ring and substitutes.

rows: rules out all the linear structures; ring with equivalent positions
All six C–C bonds identical in length
between single and double; resonance hybrid
Does not react with HCl, HBr, HOCl, cold KMnO<sub>4</sub>
calc −384 vs −208 → 176 kJ/mol (use data given in the question)

blocks.text: Resonance: true structure is a hybrid of Kekulé canonical forms of equal energy with no charge separation. Kekulé proposed the ring in 1865.
Electrophilic substitution: mechanism template (3 lines)

rows: ring + NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> → intermediate (H and NO<sub>2</sub> on same C)
AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> takes H<sup>+</sup> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub>
AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> takes H<sup>+</sup> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>R + HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub>
AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> takes H<sup>+</sup> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COR + HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub>

lines: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a catalyst (a Lewis acid): it is regenerated. Halogen carriers polarise the halogen molecule.
Further nitration / halogenation is harder and gives a mixture of 1,2- and 1,4- (notes) / 1,3-dinitrobenzene for nitration.

blocks.title: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution
blocks.task: A student suggests benzene should react with bromine like an alkene by addition. Explain why substitution is favoured instead.
steps: Benzene has a delocalised π-electron system and all six C–C bonds are equivalent.
An addition reaction would break the delocalised system and lose its stabilisation.
In electrophilic substitution, a hydrogen is replaced and the aromatic ring is restored.
blocks.answer: Benzene favours substitution because it preserves or restores its stable delocalised ring; addition would destroy that stabilisation.

items: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 111 °C; less poisonous than benzene, so used instead of benzene.
CH<sub>3</sub> activates the ring: substitution is easier than for benzene.
Nitration gives 2-nitro- and 4-nitromethylbenzene; further nitration → 2,4,6-trinitromethylbenzene (TNT, explosive).

blocks.title: UV vs catalyst
lines: Cl<sub>2</sub> + UV light → SIDE CHAIN (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl, then CHCl<sub>2</sub>, CCl<sub>3</sub>). Cl<sub>2</sub> + AlCl<sub>3</sub>/Fe → RING.

blocks.text: Hydrolysis of the side-chain halides: CH<sub>2</sub>Cl → CH<sub>2</sub>OH (benzyl alcohol); CHCl<sub>2</sub> → CHO (benzaldehyde); CCl<sub>3</sub> → COOH (benzoic acid). Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, reflux oxidises alcohol → aldehyde → acid.

blocks.title: Choose where chlorine reacts
blocks.task: Methylbenzene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> under UV light. Identify whether the ring or side chain reacts and give the first substitution product.
steps: UV light initiates free-radical substitution in the methyl side chain.
One hydrogen on the CH<sub>3</sub> group is replaced by chlorine.
Keep the benzene ring unchanged and write the HCl by-product.
blocks.answer: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (benzyl chloride) + HCl; chlorination starts on the side chain.

items: sp hybridised, linear; two π bonds at right angles; very weakly acidic ≡C–H.
Burns with a smoky luminous flame (high carbon content); used in oxy-acetylene welding.
Halogenation: Cl<sub>2</sub> in the dark → 1,2-dichloroethene → 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane; Cl<sub>2</sub> in sunlight → 2C + 2HCl (explosive).
HX reactivity: HF < HCl < HBr < HI. HI at room temp; HBr at 100 °C; HCl needs HgCl<sub>2</sub> catalyst. Excess HBr → 1,1-dibromoethane (Markovnikov).

blocks.title: Identify a terminal alkyne
blocks.task: A gas is suspected to be ethyne. Describe the confirmatory test for its terminal ≡C–H bond and state the observation.
steps: Choose ammoniacal copper(I) chloride for a terminal alkyne test.
Expose a small sample of the gas to the reagent.
A terminal alkyne reacts to form a copper(I) dicarbide precipitate.
blocks.answer: Ethyne gives a red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu(I) chloride.

sections.title: Before the test: check with your teacher

lines: HOCl + propene: your notes put Cl on the middle carbon; the usual answer is CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (Cl<sup>+</sup> to the carbon with more H).
Ethyne vs ethene test: use ammoniacal Cu(I) chloride (your notes name Fehling's solution).
Sulphonation electrophile is SO<sub>3</sub> (your notes list HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>).
Alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> hydroxylation: your notes say reflux; it is usually done cold and dilute.
